title: Grade 1 Mental Maths Addition: 4 Tricks to Add in Your Head + Free Quiz
meta_title: Grade 1 Mental Maths Addition: 4 Head Tricks
meta_desc: Grade 1 mental maths addition: making ten, doubles, counting on and the add-9 trick to add 11 to 18 in the head. Free quiz plus printable practice.
excerpt: Once the answer crosses ten, fingers run out. Here are the four mental addition tricks I use to get six-year-olds adding 11 to 18 in their heads, with a worked walk-through for each and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Watch a Grade 1 child add 8 and 5 and you will usually see the same thing: eight fingers, then a stuck look, because there are only two fingers left and the answer needs five more. That wall — the moment the sum crosses ten — is exactly where grade 1 mental maths addition either takes off or stalls. Fingers work beautifully up to ten. Past ten they run out, and the child needs a trick that lives in the head instead.

This post is only about those head tricks, and only about the sums that cross ten: the 11 to 18 range where 7 + 6, 9 + 4 and 8 + 5 live. If your child is still finding sums up to ten, start there first. But if they can add within ten and are now stuck at the ten-line, these four mental addition tricks for kids are the ones I reach for, roughly in this order.

Trick 1: Making ten (bridging)

This is the big one. To add across ten, you break the smaller number into two parts — the part that completes ten, and whatever is left over. It sounds abstract; a worked walk-through makes it obvious.

8 + 5, out loud: ‘8 needs 2 more to make 10. I take 2 from the 5, which leaves 3. So 8 + 5 becomes 10 + 3, and that is 13.’ The child never counts past ten one at a time — they jump to ten in one move, then add the leftover. This is why the pairs that make ten (2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6) must be automatic before you teach this. Making ten leans on them completely.

Model it with a ten-frame and a few loose counters for a week before expecting your child to do it alone. It feels slow at first and then, quite suddenly, it does not.

Trick 2: Doubles and near-doubles

Children learn doubles almost like a rhyme — 5 and 5 is 10, 6 and 6 is 12, 7 and 7 is 14. Once a double is locked in, the sum right next to it comes for free.

6 + 7, out loud: ‘6 and 6 is 12. 7 is just one more than 6, so 6 + 7 is one more than 12 — that is 13.’ Treating 6 + 7 as a near-double is far kinder than counting on seven separate steps. The same trick handles 7 + 8 (double 7 is 14, plus 1 is 15) and 8 + 9 (double 8 is 16, plus 1 is 17). Any two numbers that sit next to each other are a near-double waiting to happen.

Trick 3: Counting on from the bigger number

Counting on is the gentlest of the four, and it is the right tool when the smaller number is genuinely small — a 1, 2 or 3. The rule I drill hard: always start from the bigger number.

2 + 9, out loud: ‘Put the 9 in my head, then hop up two: 10, 11.’ Two hops, done. Counting on from the 2 instead would mean nine hops and far more chances to slip. Children find it genuinely funny that 2 + 9 and 9 + 2 land in the same place — and that little discovery, that order does not matter in addition, is worth more than the answer itself.

Trick 4: Adding 9 by adding 10, then taking 1

Nine is a nuisance to count and a joy to trick. Because 9 is just one short of 10, you add the easy 10 and then step back one.

9 + 4, out loud: ‘9 is nearly 10. I add 10 to the 4 to get 14, then take away the 1 I borrowed — 13.’ This same move works for adding 8 (add 10, take 2) once your child is confident. It is my favourite because it turns the scariest-looking sums, the ones with a 9 in them, into the easiest.

Which trick, when?

Part of real fluency is choosing the right trick, not knowing one and forcing it on every sum. Here is how I match them up.

StrategyWhen to use itWorked example
Making ten (bridging)Any sum crossing ten where neither number is tiny8 + 5 → 10 + 3 = 13
Doubles & near-doublesThe two numbers are equal or one apart6 + 7 → 12 + 1 = 13
Counting on from the biggerThe smaller number is 1, 2 or 32 + 9 → 9, 10, 11
Add 9 as add 10, take 1One of the numbers is 9 (or 8)9 + 4 → 14 − 1 = 13

How to practise without fingers creeping back

The hardest part is not teaching the tricks — it is stopping the fingers from sneaking back the moment you look away. A few things that help in my experience with six-year-olds:

  • Ask the child to say the trick out loud before they say the answer. ‘Nine plus four… add ten, take one… thirteen.’ The talking is the thinking.
  • Keep sessions to ten minutes. Mental maths tires young children fast, and a tired child reaches for fingers.
  • Mix the sums so the child has to pick a trick. A worksheet where every question is a making-ten sum trains one move; a mixed set trains judgement.
  • Praise the method, not the speed. ‘You used the double — nice’ matters more than ‘fast’ at this stage.

One honest caveat: some children cling to counting on for months, and that is fine. Pushing a child onto making-ten before their bonds to ten are solid just produces wrong answers and frustration. Bonds first, always. The speed you are hoping for arrives on its own once the thinking underneath is sound — never before.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free eight-question quiz built around these exact tricks — making ten, near-doubles, counting on and the add-9 move. Let your child try each one and name the trick they used, then read the explanation together for anything they miss. quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on adding across ten in your head — making ten, near-doubles, counting on and the add-9 trick. Pick an answer, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: Making ten: 8 needs 2 more to reach 10, which leaves 3 from the 5. So 10 + 3 = 13.

questions.q: Use the add-9 trick: what is 9 + 4?
questions.explanation: Add 10, then take 1: 10 + 4 = 14, take away the borrowed 1 to get 13.

questions.q: 6 + 7 is a near-double. Which is the quick way?
questions.explanation: 6 + 7 is a near-double: double 6 is 12, and 7 is one more than 6, so add 1 to get 13.

questions.q: Count on from the bigger number: what is 2 + 9?
questions.explanation: Start from 9 and hop up twice: 10, 11. Starting from the bigger number keeps it to two hops.
Making ten: 7 needs 3 more to reach 10, which leaves 3 from the 6. So 10 + 3 = 13.
Double 7 is 14, and 8 is one more than 7, so add 1 to get 15.

questions.q: Use the add-9 trick: what is 9 + 6?
questions.explanation: Add 10, then take 1: 10 + 6 = 16, take away the borrowed 1 to get 15.

questions.q: A child has 8 stickers and gets 6 more. Use making ten: how many now?
questions.explanation: Making ten: 8 needs 2 more to reach 10, which leaves 4 from the 6. So 10 + 4 = 14.

faq.q: When is a Grade 1 child ready for mental addition across ten?
faq.a: Once they can add within ten without counting every number and they know their pairs that make ten by heart. Those bonds are the foundation the making-ten trick stands on — rush past them and the head tricks fall apart.

faq.q: How do I stop my child using fingers for sums like 8 + 5?
faq.a: Do not ban fingers — give a faster tool instead. Model making ten out loud with a ten-frame until the jump to ten becomes automatic, and ask the child to say the trick aloud before the answer. Fingers fade on their own once the head method is quicker.

faq.q: Which mental trick should I teach first?
faq.a: Making ten, because most crossing-ten sums use it and it reinforces the bonds to ten your child already needs. Add doubles and near-doubles next, then the counting-on and add-9 shortcuts for the sums they suit.

faq.q: Is it a problem if my child is slow at first?
faq.a: No. Reasoning out 9 + 4 in a few seconds using add-ten-take-one is a far stronger place to be than a rote-memorised answer with no method behind it. Speed follows understanding; it never leads it.
